 Simba does not contest unauthorised spectrum use, other licence breaches; director set to resign
 Simba has informed Singapore's regulatory authorities of the circumstances surrounding the unauthorised use of the spectrum bands and the remediation steps to prevent recurrence.

 SINGAPORE: Teleco Simba "does not contest" several regulatory breaches, including the unauthorised use of spectrum bands and 5G equipment, its parent company Tuas Limited said on Tuesday (Nov 17). 
 In an announcement to the Australian Securities Exchange, Tuas said Simba had responded on Monday to a show cause notice issued by Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) on Oct 23. 
 Tuas added that, subject to regulatory approval, Mr Richard Tan will resign as a director of Simba, with new directors to be appointed. 
 Tuas had disclosed last month that IMDA issued Simba a notice to show cause, setting out six allegations involving unauthorised spectrum use, breaches of telecommunications regulations and concerns about the company's governance and compliance practices.
 In the notice posted on Tuesday, Tuas said that Simba did not contest several allegations related to unauthorised spectrum use and radio access network equipment. 
 The uncontested allegations were: 
 the unauthorised use of 2100 MHz band spectrum for 4G 
 the unauthorised use of 2340-2360 MHz band spectrum 
 the unauthorised use of 5G Indoor radio access network equipment 
 These were in breach of various licences held by Simba and the breach of the document production order, said Tuas.

 It added that Simba had informed the IMDA of the circumstances surrounding the unauthorised use of the Bands and the remediation steps put in place by Simba to seek to prevent recurrence.
 "As the matter remains under consideration by the IMDA and no findings have been made or confirmed, Tuas does not intend to provide further comment on the matters raised in this announcement," said the company.
 Also read: 
 CNA Explains: What could happen to Simba customers if IMDA takes action against alleged unauthorised spectrum use? 
 CNA Explains: How radio frequency bands are regulated - and why it matters for telcos 
 IMDA first disclosed its investigation into Simba in May, saying it had uncovered a potential regulatory breach during a review process of the telco's proposed S$1.43 billion acquisition of rival M1.
 IMDA said the potential breach involved the use of radio frequency bands not assigned to Simba to provide mobile services.
 The regulator said this would amount to unauthorised use of frequency spectrum and, if established, would breach the Telecommunications Act and conditions of Simba's licence.
 IMDA also alleged that Simba's unauthorised use of radio frequency bands was intentional and approved by its senior management, and that the telco deliberately failed to fully comply with an order to produce documents.
 Simba had until Nov 16 to respond to the notice.
